newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa still hopes to host Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: South Africa still hopes to host Zaire talks.

text.p: South Africa said on Tuesday it had no official word that Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko had pulled out of peace talks it planned to host between him and rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad told a parliamentary committee that Kabila, who now controls at least half of Zaire, was willing to attend such talks as soon as South Africa sent him word to come.
"This morning I heard that Mobutu's son had made an announcement that his father's health will not allow him to travel to South Africa," Pahad said.
"Don't take that as given. We are still waiting for the official confirmation from the president's office," he said, adding:

"We have heard from Kabila that he sticks to the general gist of the discussions we had in South Africa and he is awaiting our call to come back for this summit with Mobutu...We will continue to offer South African facilities for such a summit."

South Africa, with the collaboration of U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun, has hosted several meetings with the two sides in the Zaire war, which led last week to agreement in principle on a Mobutu-Kabila summit in South Africa. At one time it was thought the meeting would take place on Wednesday, but this now appears unlikely.
Pahad said Kabila had told South Africa he was willing to hold elections within a year of stability returning to Zaire.
"Kabila on several occasions reiterated his commitment that within a year, after there's consolidation and stability, there will be elections...in which all parties will participate," he said.

Pahad said a French envoy had met President Nelson Mandela last weekend to discuss South Africa's peacemaking role. Representatives of Britain and Belgium had met members of the foreign ministry for similar discussions.
Asked about reported U.S.-French differences in dealing with Zaire, Pahad said:
"It is our objective to ensure that any rivalry between any countries does not manifest itself in how the problems of Zaire are solved because that would be a recipe for disaster."
Pahad said the war in Zaire, one of the richest African countries in mineral resources, posed great dangers to its nine neighbours and further afield.

"(The conflict) is spreading already in terms of mass migration of people...There are constant reports which add to our concern about a possible explosion," he said, citing Angola as being particularly vulnerable as it seeks to consolidate peace after its own 19-year civil war.
"There are still forces who are attempting to see whether the crisis in Zaire can allow for conditions for the crisis to be intensified in Angola," he said.
Pahad told the committee his government was concerned at reports of mercenaries from South Africa heading for Zaire and was doing what it could to dissuade anyone from going there to fight.
There were no immediate plans to evacuate South African diplomats from Kinshasa, Pahad said. Diplomats' families and non-essential staff were withdrawn by South Africa 10 days ago.
